full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: This Rule arises upon an application filed by the accused petitioners under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings in Court Case No. 520(1) of 1995 pending in the Court of Magistrate 1st Class, Tangail.

2. Complainant-opposite Party No.1 made a complaint before, the court of Magistrate, Tangail against accused petitioners alleging, inter alia, that they in collusion with each other created a forged order purported to be made by then Munsif, 3rd Court, Tangail in Miscellaneous Case No.337 of 1973 under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, for correction of the record of right in respect of the case land, that subsequently the petitioners filed the said forged order before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur for correcting the record of rights in their favour, that pursuant thereto, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued notice upon the complainant who on enquiry ascertained that petitioners filed a forged copy of the order of the learned Munsif and thereupon filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for attaching the said forged order of the learned Munsif for drawing up a proceeding under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) refused to make any complaint and directed the complainant to file case against the accused and accordingly, complaint was made.

3. The learned Magistrate examined the complainant on 31-12-94 and sent the complaint to the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for enquiry and report. Thereafter on the basis of enquiry report, the learned Magistrate by order dated 13-7-95 took cognizance of offence under sections 467/471/109 of the Penal Code against petitioners on 13-7-95.

4. Me Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that complaint clearly discloses an offence alleged to have been committed before Revenue Court in a Mutation Proceeding before whom alleged forged Judgment of the learned Munsif was filed by them and therefore, the learned Magistrate has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of offence under sections 467/471/109 of the Penal Code against petitioners unless a formal complaint is made by the said Revenue Court in that section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure debars a criminal court from taking cognizance of such offences on the basis of private complaint. The learned Advocate further submits that since the Assistant Commissioner (Land) refused to make a complaint who is the only person to form an opinion whether the offence was committed or not, the proceeding initiated at the instance of a private person is an abuse of the process of the Court. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has cited a decision in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar and others vs Radhakanta Sarkar and others, reported in 44 DLR 533 and the case of Noor Ahmed vs Fariduddin Ahmed and others, reported in BCR 1987 (AD) 152.

5. Mr Md Amjad Hossain, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1, on the other hand, submits that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) while initiating a proceeding of mutation of the record-of-rights is not a Revenue Court within meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore, there is no legal bar in making a complaint by a private person against petitioners in respect of a forged Judgment produced by them for mutation of their names before the Revenue Officer. In support of his contention, learned Advocate has referred a decision in the case of Idris Ali and another vs State 38 DLR 270.

We have noticed that there are two conflicting decisions of this court on the said issue. Before we proceed to consider the said decisions, let us examine the provisions of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Sub-section (1) of section 195 provides 3 clauses, of them clause (c) is relevant for the disposal of the present matter. Sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 195 read as follows:

195(1)-No court shall take cognizance-

(a) .....................................

b) ......................................

(c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, except on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other court to which such Court is subordinate.

(2) In clauses <u>(b)</u> and (c) of sub-section (1) the term 'Court' includes a civil, Revenue or criminal Court but does not include a Registrar or Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act 1908.

6. Section 195(1)(c) puts an embargo of taking of cognizance by a Court of offence specified in that clause i.e. offence described in section 463 or offence punishable under section 471 or 475 or section 476 of the Penal Code which are committed in or in relation to proceedings in Court and specified procedure and method for filing complaint by a Court has been laid down in section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The ingredients of section 195(1)(c) are that an offence committed by a party to proceeding in any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court and that the alleged offence. i.e the forged deed, has been used in that court by a party to the proceeding. In respect of these offences legislature has purposely put a restriction on the general jurisdiction of a Criminal Court to take cognizance except on a complaint made by the court concerned. The purpose for which the restriction was imposed is that, that Court which is in better position to form an opinion on materials before it whether in the interest of justice, it is necessary to make a complaint against the person or persons who have committed the offence.

7. According to the complainant, the alleged fraudulent order of the learned Munsif has been used by the accused petitioners before the Assistant Commissioner (land) in a mutation proceeding and therefore, the complainant has no locus-standi to make a complaint for the offence alleged to have been committed and that the learned Magistrate also has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence on the basis of complaint made by the private person, unless the complaint is made by the Court concerned.

8. Now the question is a Revenue Officer, in the instant case Assistant Commissioner (Land), dealing with a Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court within the meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shortly the Code. In the Code, no definition of the "Revenue Court" has been given. Since there is no definition of Revenue Court in the Code, let us examine other Laws as to the meaning of the term 'Revenue Court. In the Tenancy Law i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there is no definition of Revenue Court." The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act only speaks of "Revenue Officer" includes "any officer whom the government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 provide the procedure of preparation of the records of rights by the Revenue officer. Sub- section 9(a) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act defines the term "Chief Revenue Officer" means the National Board of Revenue constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972, (president's Order 76 of 1972). Since there is no definition of "Revenue Court" in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the General Clauses Act let us examine the meaning of the term "Court." Section 6 of the Code describes classes of criminal Courts, namely:

i. Courts of Sessions:

ii. Metropolitan Magistrates:

iii. Magistrates of the first class:

iv. Magistrate of the second class:

v. Magistrates of the third class.

So, in the Code itself, there is classification of Criminal Courts only. In the Penal Code the term "Court of Justice" is defined in section 20:

"20. The words "Court of Justice" denote a Judge who is empowered by law to act judicially alone, or a body of Judges which is empowered by law to act judicially as a body, when such Judge or body of Judges is acting judicially."

In section 3 of the Evidence Act the term "Court" includes "all Judges and Magistrates and all persons, except arbitrators, legally authorised to take evidence." The word evidence means and includes "(1) all statements which the Court permits or requires to be made before it by witnesses, in relation to matters of fact under inquiry : such statements are called oral evidence; (2) all documents produced for the inspection of the Court, such documents are called documentary evidence."

Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edition points out the word 'Court' originally meant the King's place but subsequently acquired the meaning of (I) a place where justice was administered and (2) the person or persons who administer it. In the Evidence Act it is defined as including all Judges and Magistrates and all persons except arbitrators legally authorised to take evidence. This definition is by, no means exhaustive and has been framed only for the purposes of the Act. There can be no doubt that to be a Court, the person or persons who constitute it must be entrusted with judicial functions, that is, of deciding litigated questions according to law. However, by agreement between parties arbitrators may be called upon to exercise judicial powers and to decide a dispute according to law but that would not make the arbitrators a Court. It appears to me that before a person or persons can be said to constitute a court, it must be held that they derive their powers from the State and are exercising the judicial powers of the State."

9. In RV London County Council (1931) 2 KB 215 Saville LC gave the following meaning to the word "court" or "judicial authority"

"It is not necessary that it would be a court in the sense that this court is a court! It is enough if it is exercising, after hearing evidence, judicial functions in the sense that it has to decide on evidence between a proposal and an opposition; and it is not necessary to be strictly a court; if it is a tribunal which has to decide rightly after hearing evidence and opposition. "

Corpus Juris Secundum defines the word 'Court' generally

"Broadly speaking a court is a judicial tribunal engaged in the administration of justice, although the precise meaning of the term in any particular connection will vary with the context in which it is employed. ............ "A court has also been defined as a place where justice is judicially administered."

"Broadly speaking a court of law is any tribunal duly administering the laws of the land, although in a narrower sense it is a tribunal proceeding according to the common law in contradistinction to a court of equity, which latter is a tribunal proceeding according to the precepts of chancery and sometimes called a "court of conscience".

In the broad sense of the term, a court of law is any duly constituted tribunal administering the laws of the state or nation. In a narrower sense courts of law are those which administer justice according to the principles and forms of the common law, while courts of equity are those which administer justice according to the rules and principles of equity.

" ....................................................................."Civil courts are those determining controversies between private persons, and criminal courts are those adjudicating offences alleged to have been committed against the state."

Supreme Courts of India and Pakistan have endorsed the definition of "court" as above.

10. An analysis of the different laws regarding the meaning of the term "Court" and the opinion of authors on the subject makes it clear that a court must be entrusted with judicial functions. A judicial decision presupposes an existing dispute between the parties and if the dispute or a question of fact, the ascertainment of the fact by means .of evidence adduced by them to the dispute and a decision of the whole matter by finding upon the facts in dispute and the application of law to the facts so found.

11. Keeping in mind the definition of "Court" as discussed above, let us now examine whether a Revenue Officer passing an order in a mutation proceeding is a "Revenue Court" or not. If the answer is in the affirmative, then no criminal case can be launched by a private individual in any criminal court for an offence alleged to have been committed in a mutation proceeding. But if the answer is found negative, then a complaint can be launched by a private individual or an aggrieved person and the criminal court also can take cognizance on the basis of such complaint. At the outset it may be pointed out that there are conflicting decisions on the issue. One view is that a Revenue officer dealing with Mutation Proceeding is not a "Revenue court (case of Idris Ali-Supra). The contrary view is taken in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker & others (Supra). Before considering the said decisions, let us examine the relevant laws.

12. As pointed out earlier, the term revenue court has not been defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said .Act only speaks of Revenue Officer. A Revenue Officer initiates a Mutation Proceeding in exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition .and Tenancy Act 1950 and the Rules framed thereunder. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, provides:

143. Maintainability of the Record-of- rights. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under part IV, or under this part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of-(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance;

<u>(b)</u> the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings;

(c) the new settlement of lands or of holdings purchased by the Government; and

(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvion or acquisition of land.

For carrying out purposes of the Act, the Government promulgated the Tenancy Rules 1954 in exercise of powers conferred under section 152 of the Act. In the said Rules, Rules 22 and 23 provide the procedures and the manner in which the record of rights referred to In section 143 shall be maintained. The relevant portions of Rules 22 and 23 are reproduced below-

"22. Duties of Tahsildars:-(1) The Tahsildar or perwari shall be primarily responsible for reporting promptly to the Revenue Officer all changes in the ownership of land, all cases of alluvion, diluvion and reformation of land

shall also promptly bring to the notice of the Revenue Officer. . .. .. . . . . .. .

and cases of extinguishment of the interest of tenants under clauses (a)(c) and (d) of sub-section (I) of section 92 or under the second proviso to sub-section (4) of section 90 of the Act.

(2) In the cases of succession, intestate or testamentary, the report shall contain the names and addresses of all heirs and their respective shares The report shall also state if any area of land inherited by any heir is acquirable under section 91 of the Act.

(3)

(4) "In the case of apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights, the report shall state the mouza and Khatian number of the holding to which such mistakes relate.

Rule 23. Duties of Revenue Officers:

2(1) The Revenue-officer shall, if he is vested with necessary powers in this behalf under the Act, incorporate, and, if he is not vested with such powers, send up proposals to the officer vested with such powers for incorporating necessary changes in the record-of-rights,-

(a) When mutation of names is allowed as a result of inheritance either on report of the Tahsilder under rule 22 or on application of the heirs or otherwise.

<u>(b)</u> When mutation of names is made as a result of transfer on receipt of the notice of transfer under section 89 of the Act.

(c)

(d)

(2)

(3) The Revenue-Officer shall, either on application or on receipt of a report under sub-rule (1) of rule 22, for the correction of apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of- rights, after consulting the previous settlement records and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary, direct correction of such clerical mistakes,

(4) The Revenue-officer shall, either on application or on receipt of a report under clause (i) of sub-rule (1), for the correction of an entry and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry, and his act in doing so being a ministerial act, shall not be open to appeal.

<u>13. These Rules clearly provide that when Tahsilder primarily responsible for. report to the Revenue Officer apparently makes clerical mistake in record-of-rights, changes of ownership, etc., the Revenue Officer shall direct correction of such clerical mistakes and making such inquiries as he "may consider necessary direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act being a ministerial act shall not be open to appeal. A Revenue Officer holding an inquiry in a mutation proceeding, in the premises, does not become a court as he does not really adjudicate a right and he does not give a decision which is binding on the parties. He merely corrects apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights and directs correction of such clerical mistakes. If he is vested with necessary powers, incorporates necessary changes in the record-of-rights mutating the names when mutation is asked for as a result of inheritance on the report of Tahsilder under Rule 22 and also when mutation is asked for as a result of transfer, his acts being ministerial acts, shall not be open to appeal as provided in Rule 23 sub-rule (4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1954. He certainly exercises no judicial function. The functions are much more in the nature of a fiscal enquiry for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immovable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence than the revenue for which will be paid. Inquiry in mutation proceedings, therefore, being a fiscal inquiry conducted by agents of the State, for their own purposes, it could by no means be described as judicial proceeding. Therefore, a Revenue Officer when dealing with a mutation proceedings does not constitute a "Revenue Court" within the wider meaning of section 195(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.</u>

14. Now let us examine the decisions referred by the learned advocates. In the case of Idris Ali and another (supra), a Division Bench of this Court following the decisions in the case of SM Lutfullah vs Bibi Badrunnessa 20 DLR 1019, Nirman Singh vs Thakur-Ill Rudra Protop Narain Singh, AIR 1926 PC 100, Malik Fatch Khan vs Nazibullali Khan-9 DLR, WP (Lahore) 40 and Thari vs Mohammad and 2 others, PLD 1973 (SC) 619, held that:

"We are in full agreement with the view expressed in the aforesaid decisions. We are, therefore, of the opinion that a Revenue Officer dealing with a mutation proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Rules framed thereunder does not constitute a court. Since we have found that a Revenue Officer acting under Rule 23 of the Tenancy Rules is not a Court, it is needless for us to dilate on the question whether he is a civil, criminal or Revenue Court."

15. In the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar and others (Supra) another Division Bench following the decision in the case of Nur Ahmed vs Kalimuddin Ahmed and another, BCR 1987 (AD) 152, took contrary view and held that:

"We respectfully disagree with the above views of the Division Bench which held that Revenue Officer doing mutation matter is not a Revenue Court. Tenancy Rules 30 and 31 deal with preparation of record-of-rights and Tenancy Rules 20-24 deal with correction of records of right by way of Mutation. Both the matters are dealt with by the Revenue Officers and regarding Mutation matter there is a provision for review to the Revenue Officer. Weare of the view that the principle applicable to preparation of record of right also be applicable to the mutation of name in the record of rights inasmuch as both relate to preparation, modification, addition or alteration of record of rights. Relying upon the principles as laid down by the Appellate Division in above decision reported in BCR 1987 (AD) 152, we hold that the Revenue Officer dealing in Mutation of the name in the record of rights is also a Revenue Court. As we are holding this view relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division, we need not refer this matter to a Full Bench for our disagreement with another Division Bench."

16. The said decision of the Division Bench in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker was mainly based upon the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) holding that since the Appellate Division has settled the point, the learned Judge felt it not necessary to refer the matter to a Full Bench for settling the point. Let us now examine the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) and if the decision of the Appellate Division is exactly on the point, then certainly the said decision is binding on us and we are bound to follow that decision. In the Appellate Division's case, a complaint was lodged by a care-taker of Kodam Mobarak and Adam Rasul Waqf Estate before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong to the effect that he received a notice from the Objection Officer of Settlement Department and pursuant thereto, on query came to learn that accused had filed an objection case alleging that he has purchased the land in dispute and filed the deed before the objection officer, which was a forged deed. The complainant brought to the notice of the Objection Officer about the said forgery whereupon the Objection Officer seized the kabala. Accordingly, the learned Magistrate issued process upon the accused persons under sections 467/468/109 of the Penal Code. In the said case the Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1954 held that:

"Reading the provisions of Rules 30 and 39 ,of the Tenancy Rules 1954, there could be no difficulty in holding that Mr Golam Mostafa, the Objection Officer was functioning as a Revenue Court while the alleged document was placed before him in connection with proceeding under Rule 30 of the said Tenancy Rules and as such, section 195(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is clearly attracted which puts an embargo on taking cognizance of the alleged offence under sections 467 and 468 of the Penal Code in the absence of a complaint from the court concerned".

17. In the Appellate Division's case the issue was whether an Objection Officer having power of an Assistant Settlement Officer in deciding Objection Petition is a Revenue Court or not. The Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 held that a Revenue Officer having additional powers of Settlement Officer while hearing objection case shall have all powers exercisable by a civil court in a trial of suits under Civil Procedure Code and decides ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land and therefore, the objection officer is functioning as a "Revenue Court". These Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose and the manner in which revision of the record-of-rights can be prepared under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 144 provides:

"(1) The Government may in any case if it thinks fit make an order directing that a record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or local area be prepared or revised by a Revenue Officer in accordance with such rules as may be made by the Government in this

behalf;

(2)

(3) A notification in the Official Gazette of an order under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence that the order has been duly made.

(4)

(5)

(6) Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Revenue-Officer on any objection made under sub-section (5) may prefer an appeal to the prescribed Revenue Authority hot below the rank of an Assistant Settlement Officer in such manner and within such period as may be prescribed.

(7) When all such objections and appeals have been considered and disposed of according to such rules as the Government may make in this behalf, the Revenue-Officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause such record to be finally published in the prescribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this section.

(8)

<u>18. Relevant portions of Rules 29, 30, 31, 35, 36 and 39 are reproduced below which would give us a complete answer on the issue.</u>

<u>"29 Publication of draft record of rights:</u>

<u>"30. Objection ....................................</u>

<u>objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue Officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties naturally interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue Officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned.</u>

<u>31 Appeal: (1) Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Revenue Officer on any objection made under rule 30 may appeal to the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Assistant Settlement Officer .......................................</u>

<u>(2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision.</u>

<u>"35 Presumption as to the correctness of record-of-rights: (1) When a record of rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act."</u>

<u>(2) ................................</u>

<u>36. Power vested in Revenue Officers:</u>

<u>(a) the power to take down evidence in his own hand in English language in proceedings held under the said chapter in which an appeal is allowed, in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for trial of suits: and</u>

<u>(b)</u>

<u>"39 Further powers vested in Settlement and Assistant Settlement Officers: A Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation "Settlement Officer" or "Assistant Settlement Officer" shall have all powers exercisable by a civil court in the trial of suits under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (Act V of 1908).</u>

<u>These rules are included in chapter VII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 under the heading "Revision of record of rights under section 144 of the Act." This chapter deals with the particulars to be recorded at the stages of the work, procedure of work up to attestation, publication of draft record of rights, objection, appeal, publication of final records, certificate of final publication, presumption as to correctness of record of rights, powers of Revenue Officers, etc. while revising the record-of-rights under section 144 of the Act. After such revision of the record-of-rights at the instance of the Government of any district, part of a district or local area by the Revenue Officer appointed for the purpose who shall have either with or without the additional designation of "Settlement Officer", or "Assistant Settlement Officer", such Revenue Officer shall publish a draft record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection at such convenient place as he may determine and a proclamation be published informing the tenants/maliks for filing objections. After hearing the objections, if any, he shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. Similarly, in case of an appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. The provisions of Act and the Rules clearly show that the revision of the record-of-rights made under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has' presumptive value, but any order of mutation of the record made under section 143 of the Act has no such presumptive value. A Revenue Officer appointed with the power of Settlement Officer shall have all powers exercisable by a Civil Court in the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure. These Rules and the rules framed by the Governor in Council of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 are closely akin Rule 36 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 is similar to Rule 41 of the Bengal Rules. Similarly, Rules 39 and 40 are equivalent to Rules 44 and 45 of Bengal Rules. The Bengal Government Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose of chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It is settled that the record of rights prepared in chapter I of the Bengal Tenancy Act i.e. under sections 101-104 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have the presumptive value as in section 144 of the Act but such presumption is not available in section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the Appellate Division's case no argument was made as to whether a Revenue Officer dealing with Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court or not and naturally the Appellate Division has not decided the said issue. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed is quite distinguishable from the facts of the case of Idris Ali (38 DLR 270) and the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (44 DLR 533). The Appellate Division case was decided upon consideration of the Rules contained in Chapter VII and VIII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 which were framed in exercise of section 152(2)(2b) of the Act, for carrying out the purposes for all or any of the provisions of section 144 of the Act which the facts in the case of Idris Ali (Supra) and that of Ajit Kumar Sarkar(Supra) are similar to the present case, which relate to mutation proceedings under section 143 of the Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 framed in exercise of section 152 (2)(2a) of the Act. In the premises aforesaid, we are in respectful agreement with the views taken by the Division of the High Court Division in the case of Idris Ali (Supra). For the reasons discussed above and the provisions of law quoted herein before, with due respect to the learned Judges of the High Court Division, we are unable to endorse the views taken by them in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (Supra).</u>

<u>19. Now the question is on the face of two conflicting decisions on the issue this court exercising co-ordinate jurisdiction can decide the issue without referring the matter to a larger Bench or leaving the point to be decided by the Appellate Division. We are conscious that when a Division Bench of a High Court Division is not inclined to take a view from that of an earlier judgment of a similar Division Bench the matter should be referred to a larger Bench. In this connection we are referring to a decision in the case of the Province of East Pakistan and others vs Sirajul Huq Patwari and others reported in 19 DLR (SC) 281.</u>

<u>"Where a Division Bench of the High Court is inclined to take a different view from that declared in an earlier judgment of a similar Division Bench one course open to the Court was to "have expressed their doubts regarding the view taken in the precedent case a Court of co-equal jurisdiction, while yet following that view, and left the matter to be raised in appeal before this Court (Supreme Court)" A single judge or a Division Court possesses the full force of a decision of the High Court, and is subject only to modification or correction by proper appeal to the Supreme Court, except in the few cases where provision is made by the Letters Patent for an appeal or other mode of variation within the High Court, in which case the latter decision would possess the full force of a decision by the High Court, and would be amenable to appeal by this Court."</u>

<u>20. It has been pointed out earlier that the High Court Division, in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker and others (Supra) based its decision relying upon the case of the Appellate Division, the facts of which are quite distinguishable from the case of the case reported in the case of Noor Ahmed and the High Court Division without examining the relevant provisions of law i.e. section 143 of the Act and chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954, held that a "Revenue Officer" dealing with mutation proceeding is a "Revenue Court." Therefore, we are unable to approve the views taken in that case and consequently, we are of the opinion that the matter need not be referred for decision to a larger Bench since there is earlier decision of a Division bench over the said issue, with whom we are in full agreement. Accordingly, we approve the decision of the Division Bench in the case of Idris Ali. Our view is that a Revenue Officer when dealing with a Mutation Proceeding does not constitute a Revenue Court within the meaning of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore, a Criminal Court can take cognizance of any offence described in sections 463 and 471, 475 and 476 of the Penal Code on the basis of complaint filed by any aggrieved party when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any Mutation proceeding in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. Accordingly, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.</u>

21.	The Rule is, therefore, discharged.

22.	The stay order granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

23. Send down the lower court records.

The ad-interim bail granted to the petitioner Nos. 15-19 Md Jaher Ali, Md Sadeque Ali, Md Abdul Karim, Md Amir Ali and Md Emran Ali are hereby confirmed in the facts and circumstances of the case.

End.
